output_text:
It’s understandable to feel nervous. Choosing a career can sound like a one-time decision that determines your whole life, but most people don’t discover one perfect fit and then follow a straight path forever. Work changes, people change, and skills from one role often transfer to another. You’re making a next-step decision, not signing a lifetime contract.

You may not need to find a career that feels like a calling. A good-enough fit can offer some combination of tolerable day-to-day tasks, decent working conditions, financial stability, and room to grow. It’s also okay if work is not the main source of meaning in your life.

Instead of trying to decide from a distance, gather evidence. Talk with people doing work that interests you, ask what an ordinary week is really like, and try a class, volunteer project, short placement, or small related task if you can. Notice which activities give you energy, which drain you, and what conditions matter to you—such as structure, autonomy, teamwork, or predictable hours. A career choice is easier when it’s based on experience rather than pressure to predict the future perfectly.

You can also make the decision smaller: choose a course, first job, or experiment that builds useful skills and keeps options open. Set a time to review how it’s going, rather than expecting certainty before you begin. If anxiety is making every option feel impossible, talking it through with a trusted person or career adviser may help you separate practical concerns from fear.

You don’t have to feel completely sure to take a sensible next step.

output_text:
At 16, you don’t need a long resume or professional-level skills. Employers hiring for entry-level work generally want someone dependable, polite, willing to learn, and able to show up when scheduled. Look for postings that say “entry-level,” “no experience necessary,” or “training provided,” and consider grocery stores, restaurants, recreation centers, camps, tutoring, pet care, or seasonal work. Some online listings describe an ideal candidate rather than strict requirements, so you can still apply if you meet most of the basics.

Keep your resume to one page. Put your name and contact information at the top, then a short summary such as “Reliable high school student seeking a part-time role; available evenings and weekends.” Add your education, expected graduation date, and any relevant activities or experience. School projects, clubs, sports, volunteering, babysitting, helping with a family business, and community responsibilities can all demonstrate useful skills. Describe what you actually did: for example, “Organized supplies for club events” or “Cared for children and followed parents’ instructions.” Include skills you can honestly support, such as customer service, teamwork, punctuality, basic computer use, or a second language. Don’t invent experience or list references on the resume; you can say “References available upon request” or provide them separately if asked.

Ask teachers, coaches, volunteer coordinators, or other adults who know your reliability whether they’d be comfortable serving as references. Give them a heads-up before sharing their contact details. Check each employer’s minimum-age rules and your local requirements for work permits, permitted hours, and school-day limits; a parent or school counselor can help you find out what applies.

Before applying, practice a brief introduction and a few interview answers about why you want the job, when you’re available, and how you handle responsibility. Apply to several suitable openings, follow instructions carefully, and politely check in if you haven’t heard back after about a week. Your first job is mainly a chance to build a record of reliability and learn.

content.text:
Look at the overlap between what you enjoy, what you’re good at or willing to learn, and what kind of life you want your work to support. Interest matters, but so do everyday realities: typical tasks, working hours, stress, job security, pay, location, and opportunities to progress. A career can sound appealing from the outside yet feel very different once you understand the daily work.

Try to learn about roles directly. Talk with people doing the work, ask what a normal week looks like, and, where possible, try a class, project, internship, volunteer role, or short placement. Pay attention not only to what you like, but also to what you find draining. Research the qualifications and costs involved, and check whether demand for the work is likely to fit your needs.

You don’t have to identify one perfect path for life. Many people change direction as their interests and circumstances develop, and skills often transfer between fields. Choose a sensible next step that gives you useful experience and keeps options open. If you’re undecided, compare a few possibilities against your priorities rather than waiting for complete certainty. A career decision is important, but it is rarely irreversible.

output_text:
An AOS plus real shop experience is likely the strongest next step. Start working, learn which parts of welding and fabrication you enjoy, and build a record of safety, quality, and reliability. Job prospects and pay vary by location, specialty, and experience, so treat “guaranteed jobs” as a reason to explore—not a promise.

You can pursue the BBA later, perhaps part-time or with employer support. A management degree is most useful if you want to move into supervision, project management, or operations; it may not improve your welding prospects as much as experience and targeted certifications right away.

Your work history has not permanently disqualified you, but a decade without relevant experience means employers may see your degree as stale and your recent work as unrelated. The goal is to give them current evidence that you can do the job, not to add more general certificates.

First, ask a few working engineers or an engineering recruiter in your specific discipline to review your résumé and a sample application. “ATS compliant” is not the same as clearly showing relevant skills, projects, software, and results. Tailor each application to a particular role, and don’t rely only on online postings: contact alumni, former professors, professional societies, and local engineering firms to request brief informational conversations. Referrals can help your application get read.

Build recent, demonstrable work in the field: a substantial project, contract or volunteer engineering work where appropriate, or a bridge role such as technician, test, quality, CAD, or engineering support. Check licensing or other discipline-specific requirements as well. You may need to target junior roles rather than the level implied by a master’s degree.

A 0.1% interview rate is a signal to change the targeting or presentation, not proof that your prospects are over. Track results by role type and revise based on feedback.

Your best advantage will be pairing marine biology knowledge with practical data skills. In college, look for research labs, field courses, internships, and volunteer projects with universities, aquariums, conservation groups, government agencies, and local watershed or coastal organizations. Ask faculty and career advisers about opportunities, and contact organizations with a short, specific note explaining what you can contribute and what you hope to learn.

Build a small portfolio as you go: for example, a clearly documented analysis of publicly available ocean or wildlife data, a map, or a simple visualization. Learn tools used in the field, such as R or Python, GIS, statistics, and careful data management. Strong communication matters too; practice explaining findings to non-specialists.

You don’t need to wait until college to explore. Attend public talks, join citizen-science projects, and speak with working professionals about their day-to-day roles and needed skills. Keep track of contacts and follow up thoughtfully. Marine biology jobs can be competitive, so stay open to related paths in ecology, fisheries, environmental consulting, and data analysis while building relevant experience.
